title: Destructuring for React
summary: Destructuring pulls values out of objects or arrays into named variables.
whenToUse: Use it constantly in React for props, hook return values, API objects, event objects, and array values.
do: Destructure props in component parameters when it improves readability.
Use array destructuring for hooks like useState.
Use clear variable names after destructuring.
dont: Do not destructure deeply if it makes the component harder to scan.
Do not destructure values before checking that optional data exists.

codeSnippets.title: Destructure component props
codeSnippets.description: React props are objects, so destructuring keeps component code short.
codeSnippets.explanation: The component receives one props object, then destructures the values it needs.

codeSnippets.title: Destructure hook return values
codeSnippets.description: useState returns a two-item array.
codeSnippets.code: const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
codeSnippets.explanation: The first array item is the current value, and the second is the setter function.

commonMistake: Destructuring nested values before the parent object exists, causing a runtime error.
interviewQuestion: Why is destructuring common in React?
interviewAnswer: React often passes data as objects or arrays, and destructuring makes it easy to pull out the exact values a component or hook needs.

courseReference.notes: The review introduces object and array destructuring before React props and hooks use the same pattern.

title: Spread, rest, and immutability
summary: Spread copies arrays or objects, while rest collects leftover values into an array or object.
whenToUse: Use spread to create new state objects or arrays instead of mutating existing state.
do: Use spread to add items to an array immutably.
Use object spread to update one property while keeping the others.
Use rest when you need the remaining values after destructuring.
dont: Do not mutate React state arrays with push, splice, or direct assignment.
Do not forget that spread is shallow.

codeSnippets.title: Add an item without mutation
codeSnippets.description: Create a new array when updating React state.
codeSnippets.code: setItems((items) => [...items, newItem]);
codeSnippets.explanation: React receives a new array reference, so it can detect that state changed.

codeSnippets.title: Update one object in an array
codeSnippets.description: Map over the array and copy only the item that changes.
codeSnippets.explanation: The unchanged items keep their identity, while the changed item becomes a new object.

commonMistake: Mutating an existing state object and then wondering why React does not update reliably.
interviewQuestion: Why is immutability important for React state?
interviewAnswer: React relies on new object or array references to understand that state changed and to keep updates predictable.

courseReference.notes: The review shows spread for copying arrays and objects, which later becomes essential for state updates.

title: Ternary and short-circuit rendering
summary: Ternaries and logical && are JavaScript expressions that are useful for conditional JSX.
whenToUse: Use a ternary when choosing between two UI branches, and use && for a small optional fragment.
do: Use ternaries for clear either-or rendering.
Use && for small optional UI.
Move complex conditions into named variables.
dont: Do not create deeply nested ternaries inside JSX.
Do not use && with values like 0 if rendering 0 would be confusing.

codeSnippets.title: Choose between two labels
codeSnippets.description: Use a ternary when both true and false branches matter.
codeSnippets.explanation: The ternary returns one string when isSaved is true and another when it is false.

codeSnippets.title: Render optional content
codeSnippets.description: Use && when you only need to show something in the true case.
codeSnippets.explanation: When error is truthy, React renders the paragraph. When it is empty, React renders nothing.

commonMistake: Using a nested ternary for complex UI instead of extracting variables or components.
interviewQuestion: How do JavaScript expressions help with conditional rendering in React?
interviewAnswer: JSX accepts expressions, so ternaries and && can return different UI based on current props or state.

courseReference.notes: The review covers ternaries and logical operators before they are used in JSX.

title: Optional chaining and nullish coalescing
summary: Optional chaining safely reads nested properties, and nullish coalescing provides defaults only for null or undefined.
whenToUse: Use them when rendering API data that may be incomplete or not loaded yet.
do: Use ?. when part of a nested object may be missing.
Use ?? when 0 or an empty string are valid values.
Prefer clear fallback text for user-facing UI.
dont: Do not use || when 0 is a valid value you want to keep.
Do not let optional chaining hide data-shape bugs that should be fixed.

codeSnippets.title: Read nested API data safely
codeSnippets.description: Avoid crashes when nested data is missing.
codeSnippets.code:
const reviewCount = book.reviews?.librarything?.reviewsCount ?? 0; return

{reviewCount} reviews

;
codeSnippets.explanation: If reviews or librarything is missing, the expression falls back to 0 instead of throwing.

codeSnippets.title: Keep valid zero values
codeSnippets.description: Use ?? when 0 should not be replaced.
codeSnippets.code: const rating = movie.userRating ?? "Not rated yet";
codeSnippets.explanation: Nullish coalescing only falls back for null or undefined, not for 0.

commonMistake: Using || for defaults and accidentally replacing valid values like 0 or an empty string.
interviewQuestion: When should you use ?? instead of ||?
interviewAnswer: Use ?? when only null or undefined should trigger the fallback, while values like 0, false, or an empty string should stay valid.

courseReference.notes: The review compares optional chaining and nullish coalescing for nested review data.

title: map, filter, and reduce
summary: map transforms arrays, filter keeps matching items, and reduce combines an array into one value.
whenToUse: Use them for rendering lists, searching, deleting items, deriving totals, and building UI data from raw data.
do: Use map to render or transform each item.
Use filter to remove or select items immutably.
Use reduce for totals and grouped values.
dont: Do not mutate arrays while deriving UI.
Do not use reduce when map or filter would be clearer.

codeSnippets.title: Render with map
codeSnippets.description: Turn an array of data into repeated JSX.
codeSnippets.code:
const rows = books.map((book) =>
  • {book.title}
    • );
codeSnippets.explanation: map returns a new array of JSX elements, and each element needs a stable key.

codeSnippets.title: Filter and total data
codeSnippets.description: Combine array methods to derive display values.
codeSnippets.code:
const longBooks = books.filter((book) => book.pages > 500);
const totalPages = longBooks.reduce((sum, book) => sum + book.pages, 0);
codeSnippets.explanation: filter creates a smaller array, and reduce turns it into a single total.

commonMistake: Using map for side effects instead of returning a transformed value.
interviewQuestion: Why is map so common in React?
interviewAnswer: React renders repeated UI from arrays, and map is the standard way to transform each data item into JSX.

courseReference.notes: The review practices map, filter, and reduce with book data before React uses them for lists and derived state.

title: Sorting without mutation
summary: Array sort mutates the original array, so copy the array before sorting React data.
whenToUse: Use this when sorting lists from props, state, API data, or derived UI collections.
do: Copy the array with slice or spread before sort.
Use a compare function for numbers and custom object fields.
Keep the original state array unchanged.
dont: Do not call sort directly on state.
Do not forget that default sort compares values as strings.

codeSnippets.title: Copy before sorting
codeSnippets.description: Avoid mutating the original array.
codeSnippets.explanation: slice creates a copy, so sort can reorder the copy without mutating state.

codeSnippets.title: Sort by numeric value
codeSnippets.description: Use subtraction for numeric sorting.
codeSnippets.code: const shortestFirst = movies.slice().sort((a, b) => a.runtime - b.runtime);
codeSnippets.explanation: The compare function tells JavaScript how to order numeric values.

commonMistake: Calling items.sort(...) directly on a state array, which mutates existing state.
interviewQuestion: Why should you copy an array before sorting it in React?
interviewAnswer: sort mutates the array, and React state should be treated as immutable, so sorting a copy avoids changing existing state directly.

courseReference.notes: The review shows slice before sort so the original array remains unchanged.

title: Immutable array updates
summary: React state arrays should be updated by creating new arrays, not by mutating the existing one.
whenToUse: Use immutable array updates for adding, deleting, toggling, and editing items in state.
do: Use spread to add an item.
Use filter to remove an item.
Use map to update one item.
dont: Do not use push, pop, splice, or direct item assignment on state arrays.
Do not update an object inside an array without copying that object.

codeSnippets.title: Add, delete, update
codeSnippets.description: Three common immutable array operations.
codeSnippets.explanation: Each operation returns a new array, and the update also returns a new object for the changed item.

commonMistake: Updating an item by changing a property on the existing object inside the array.
interviewQuestion: How do you update an item inside a React state array?
interviewAnswer: Use map to return a new array, copy the matching item with object spread, and leave all other items unchanged.

courseReference.notes: The review practices add, delete, and update operations with arrays of objects.

title: Template literals
summary: Template literals create strings with embedded expressions using backticks and ${...}.
whenToUse: Use them for readable labels, messages, dynamic class names, URLs, and small formatted strings.
do: Use template literals when a string includes variables.
Keep formatting logic simple and readable.
Move complex string building into a helper function.
dont: Do not build long UI strings with many plus operators.
Do not hide complicated conditional text inside one huge template literal.

codeSnippets.title: Create a dynamic label
codeSnippets.description: Embed expressions in a string.
codeSnippets.code:
const label = `${title} has ${pages} pages`; return

{label}

;
codeSnippets.explanation: The expressions inside ${...} are evaluated and inserted into the final string.

codeSnippets.title: Build a request URL
codeSnippets.description: Template literals are useful for small dynamic URLs.
codeSnippets.code: const url = `/api/books?query=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`;
codeSnippets.explanation: The query value becomes part of the URL while encodeURIComponent keeps it safe for a query string.

commonMistake: Forgetting that JSX expressions still need curly braces around a template literal.
interviewQuestion: Why are template literals useful in React code?
interviewAnswer: They make dynamic strings easier to read when UI text, class names, or URLs include JavaScript values.

courseReference.notes: The review uses template literals to build a book summary string.

title: Arrow functions and callbacks
summary: Arrow functions are compact functions often passed as callbacks to events and array methods.
whenToUse: Use them for event handlers that pass arguments, inline array transformations, and small helper functions.
do: Pass a function to event props instead of calling it during render.
Use arrow callbacks with map, filter, and reduce.
Extract functions when inline callbacks become hard to read.
dont: Do not write onClick={handleClick()} unless handleClick returns another function on purpose.
Do not cram complex multi-step logic into a tiny inline callback.

codeSnippets.title: Pass an argument in an event
codeSnippets.description: Wrap the function call in another function so it waits for the click.
codeSnippets.explanation: The arrow function is the event handler. It calls onSelect only when the user clicks.

codeSnippets.title: Use callbacks with array methods
codeSnippets.description: Array methods receive callback functions.
codeSnippets.code: const titles = books.map((book) => book.title);
codeSnippets.explanation: map calls the arrow function once for each book and returns a new array of titles.

commonMistake: Calling a function immediately in JSX instead of passing a callback to React.
interviewAnswer: A callback is a function passed to another function so it can be called later, such as on a click or for each array item.

courseReference.notes: The review uses arrow functions for helpers and array method callbacks.

title: Promises and async/await
summary: Promises represent future values, and async/await lets you write promise code in a readable step-by-step style.
whenToUse: Use async/await for API calls, loading data, submitting forms, and any operation that finishes later.
do: Use await inside an async function.
Wrap awaited work in try/catch when it can fail.
Remember that an async function always returns a promise.
dont: Do not expect an async function result synchronously.
Do not ignore rejected promises.

codeSnippets.title: Fetch JSON with async/await
codeSnippets.description: Wait for the response and then wait for JSON parsing.
codeSnippets.explanation: fetch returns a promise, response.json returns another promise, and await pauses this async function until each finishes.

codeSnippets.title: Use async result later
codeSnippets.description: An async function returns a promise, so handle it with await or then.
codeSnippets.explanation: The handler waits for the data before updating state and catches failures for user feedback.

commonMistake: Assigning const data = loadTodos() and expecting data to already contain the resolved array.
interviewQuestion: What does an async function return?
interviewAnswer: An async function always returns a promise, even when you return a plain value from inside it.

courseReference.notes: The review ends with fetch, promises, and async/await before API work in React effects.

title: Fetch API basics
summary: fetch starts an HTTP request and returns a promise for the response.
whenToUse: Use fetch when a React app needs to load or send data from a browser-based API request.
do: Await the fetch response before reading the body.
Check response.ok because fetch does not throw for HTTP error statuses.
Parse JSON with response.json when the API returns JSON.
dont: Do not assume fetch throws for 404 or 500 responses.
Do not forget that response.json also returns a promise.

codeSnippets.title: Load JSON data
codeSnippets.description: A small helper that gets JSON from an endpoint.
codeSnippets.explanation: The helper waits for the response, handles HTTP failures, and returns the parsed JSON promise.

codeSnippets.title: Send JSON data
codeSnippets.description: Send a JSON body with headers.
codeSnippets.explanation: POST requests usually include a method, a JSON content type, and a stringified body.

commonMistake: Catching network errors but forgetting to check response.ok for HTTP errors.
interviewQuestion: Does fetch throw an error for a 404 response?
interviewAnswer: No. fetch only rejects for network-level failures. You should check response.ok and throw your own error for bad HTTP statuses.

courseReference.notes: The review introduces fetch and async/await before React uses requests in effects.

title: JSON parse and stringify
summary: JSON is the text format most APIs and browser storage examples use to move JavaScript-like data around.
whenToUse: Use JSON.stringify before sending or saving objects, and JSON.parse when reading JSON text back into JavaScript values.
do: Use JSON.stringify for request bodies and localStorage values.
Use JSON.parse only on valid JSON strings.
Handle parse failures when stored or remote data may be invalid.
dont: Do not store raw objects in localStorage without stringifying them.
Do not assume JSON.parse can parse JavaScript syntax like comments or trailing commas.

codeSnippets.title: Stringify a request body
codeSnippets.description: Convert an object into JSON text before sending it.
codeSnippets.explanation: HTTP request bodies are text or binary data, so the object must be converted to a JSON string.

codeSnippets.title: Parse saved data
codeSnippets.description: Read a JSON string back into a JavaScript value.
codeSnippets.code:
const saved = localStorage.getItem("settings");
const settings = saved ? JSON.parse(saved) : { theme: "light" };
codeSnippets.explanation: localStorage returns strings, so JSON.parse restores the saved object shape.

commonMistake: Forgetting that localStorage stores only strings, so saved objects must be stringified and parsed.
interviewQuestion: Why do we use JSON.stringify before storing an object in localStorage?
interviewAnswer: localStorage stores strings, so JSON.stringify converts the object into a string that can later be restored with JSON.parse.

courseReference.notes: The project persists watched movies by saving structured data in browser storage.

title: Browser storage basics
summary: Browser storage can keep small string values on the user's device between page loads.
whenToUse: Use localStorage for small non-sensitive preferences, drafts, or saved UI data that should survive refreshes.
do: Store only small non-sensitive data.
Stringify objects and arrays before saving them.
Read storage in a lazy initializer or effect when using React.
dont: Do not store passwords, tokens, or private data casually in localStorage.
Do not read and parse storage on every render.

codeSnippets.title: Save a preference
codeSnippets.description: Use localStorage for a small persistent value.
codeSnippets.code:
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
const theme = localStorage.getItem("theme") ?? "light";
codeSnippets.explanation: The saved value remains available after a page refresh in the same browser.

codeSnippets.title: Save an array
codeSnippets.description: Convert structured data to JSON before saving it.
codeSnippets.code:
localStorage.setItem("watched", JSON.stringify(watchedMovies));
const watched = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("watched") ?? "[]");
codeSnippets.explanation: Arrays and objects must become strings before storage can save them.

commonMistake: Using localStorage as if it were React state instead of syncing storage with state intentionally.
interviewQuestion: When is localStorage useful in a React app?
interviewAnswer: It is useful for small non-sensitive values that should persist after refresh, usually synced through state and an effect or a custom hook.

courseReference.notes: The watched movies list is persisted between visits using browser storage.

title: const, let, and scope
summary: const and let create block-scoped variables; React code usually uses const unless a local variable must be reassigned.
whenToUse: Use const for components, props, state values, derived values, handlers, and arrays or objects whose binding should not be reassigned.
do: Use const by default for values inside components.
Use let only when the same local variable must be reassigned.
Keep variables close to the code that uses them.
dont: Do not use var in modern React code.
Do not confuse const with immutability of object contents.

codeSnippets.title: Use const for derived values
codeSnippets.description: Most component values are calculated once per render.
codeSnippets.explanation: count and label are recreated on every render, but they are not reassigned during that render.

codeSnippets.title: Use let for reassignment
codeSnippets.description: Use let only when a local value changes before rendering.
codeSnippets.explanation: The variable binding changes, so let is the right choice for this local calculation.

commonMistake: Assuming const makes an object deeply immutable; const only prevents reassigning the variable binding.
interviewQuestion: Why is const used so often in React components?
interviewAnswer: Most values in a render are calculated and then read, not reassigned, so const communicates intent and avoids accidental reassignment.

courseReference.notes: The review uses modern JavaScript variable declarations that React code relies on throughout the course.

title: Truthy, falsy, and boolean checks
summary: JavaScript conditions use truthy and falsy values, which directly affects conditional rendering in JSX.
whenToUse: Use explicit boolean checks when rendering empty states, badges, warnings, and UI that depends on data length or loaded values.
do: Check array length when you care whether a list has items.
Use clear boolean variable names like hasResults or canSubmit.
Convert unclear values with Boolean when readability helps.
dont: Do not treat an empty array as falsy; arrays are always truthy.
Do not let 0 accidentally hide or show UI without thinking about it.

codeSnippets.title: Check an array before rendering
codeSnippets.description: Use length instead of relying on the array value.
codeSnippets.explanation: An empty array is truthy, so results ? ... would not detect the empty state.

codeSnippets.title: Use a named boolean
codeSnippets.description: Make conditions easier to read in JSX.
codeSnippets.code:
const canSubmit = title.trim() !== "" && !isSaving;

return <button disabled={!canSubmit}>Save</button>;
codeSnippets.explanation: The named boolean explains the rule and keeps the JSX compact.

commonMistake: Writing items && <List /> and expecting it to hide the list when items is an empty array.
interviewQuestion: Is an empty array truthy or falsy in JavaScript?
interviewAnswer: An empty array is truthy, so check items.length when the condition depends on whether the array has elements.

courseReference.notes: The review covers logical operators and conditional expressions that become important in JSX.

title: Default values
summary: Default values keep components predictable when props, function arguments, or API fields are missing.
whenToUse: Use defaults for optional props, helper parameters, and UI fallback values that should always exist.
do: Use default parameters for optional component props.
Use ?? for fallbacks when 0, false, or an empty string are valid.
Keep fallback values close to where the data is read.
dont: Do not use || when valid falsy values should be preserved.
Do not hide required props by giving everything a default.

codeSnippets.title: Default optional props
codeSnippets.description: Destructured props can have default values.
codeSnippets.explanation: If tone or children are not provided, the component still renders with useful defaults.

codeSnippets.title: Fallback for missing API data
codeSnippets.description: Use ?? when only null or undefined should fall back.
codeSnippets.code: const displayName = user.name ?? "Anonymous user";
codeSnippets.explanation: The fallback is used only when name is null or undefined.

commonMistake: Using || for defaults and accidentally replacing valid values like 0, false, or an empty string.
interviewQuestion: How can a React component define default values for optional props?
interviewAnswer: A common approach is to destructure props in the function parameter and assign default values there.

courseReference.notes: The review introduces fallback logic that React components later use for optional data.

title: find, some, and includes
summary: find selects one matching item, some checks if any item matches, and includes checks if a primitive value exists.
whenToUse: Use these methods to select active items, check permissions, mark favorites, and derive UI flags from arrays.
do: Use find when you need one object from an array.
Use some when you only need a true or false answer.
Use includes for primitive values such as strings or ids.
dont: Do not use filter when you only need one item.
Do not use includes to compare objects by shape; it checks object references.

codeSnippets.title: Find selected data
codeSnippets.description: Use find to get the active object.
codeSnippets.code:
const selectedBook = books.find((book) => book.id === selectedId); return

{selectedBook?.title ?? "Choose a book"}

;
codeSnippets.explanation: find returns the first matching book or undefined, so optional chaining keeps the render safe.

codeSnippets.title: Check whether something exists
codeSnippets.description: Use some for objects and includes for primitive values.
codeSnippets.code:
const isFavorite = favorites.some((book) => book.id === bookId);
const hasReactTag = tags.includes("react");
codeSnippets.explanation: some runs a test for each object, while includes checks whether the exact primitive value is present.

commonMistake: Using filter(...)[0] when find communicates the intent more clearly.
interviewQuestion: What is the difference between find and filter?
interviewAnswer: find returns the first matching item, while filter returns a new array with all matching items.

courseReference.notes: The review builds array-method fluency that React uses for selecting, rendering, and deriving UI data.

title: Import and export modules
summary: Modules let JavaScript files share components, functions, data, and hooks through import and export.
whenToUse: Use modules to split React apps into components, utilities, hooks, and data files.
do: Export reusable components, hooks, and helper functions.
Use default exports for one main thing from a file when the codebase prefers it.
Use named exports when a file exposes multiple utilities.
dont: Do not put every component and helper in one large file.
Do not mix default and named imports incorrectly.

codeSnippets.title: Default export a component
codeSnippets.description: A component file often exports one main component.
codeSnippets.explanation: Another file can import this component with any local name.

codeSnippets.title: Named export a utility
codeSnippets.description: Named exports make utility imports explicit.
codeSnippets.explanation: The import name must match the exported name, which makes utility usage clear.

commonMistake: Importing a named export as if it were a default export, or the reverse.
interviewQuestion: Why do React apps use JavaScript modules?
interviewAnswer: Modules keep code organized by allowing files to export reusable pieces and import only what they need.

courseReference.notes: The review prepares the JavaScript foundation used later when React components and hooks are split across files.
